query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The enhanced corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily governed by the formation and maintenance of a dense Cr2O3-based passive oxide film that is synergistically supported by an optimized microstructure (e.g., specific grain size or phase distribution) which promotes rapid chromium diffusion to damaged areas, thereby mitigating localized corrosion even under high temperature, corrosive, and irradiative conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Steels with a typical martensitic or austenitic microstructure and a naturally formed Cr-rich passive oxide film as employed in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
generation.intervention: Prepare steel samples with deliberately varied oxide layer states (intact vs. mechanically/chemically removed) and controlled microstructural characteristics (via heat treatment to alter grain size and phase distribution). Expose these samples under simulated chemical processing conditions (e.g., high temperature, relevant corrosive salt environments) with and without a controlled dose of ionizing radiation.
generation.conditions: Simulated chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments at temperatures ranging from about 450 °C to 700 °C, with corrosive salt atmospheres (e.g., NaCl-based solutions or molten salt mixtures) and controlled radiation levels reflective of operational exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity of the Cr2O3-rich passive film and the microstructural features (grain boundary density and phase distribution) that facilitate chromium diffusion to any local damage sites.
generation.mechanism: Under service conditions, the steel’s surface rapidly forms a dense Cr2O3 passive layer that inhibits further oxidation. Simultaneously, an optimized microstructure with appropriate grain sizes serves as a reservoir for chromium that can diffuse to repair or reinforce the passive layer at sites of local disruption, especially under the dual stresses of high temperature and ionizing radiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with intact passive oxide films and optimized microstructures will exhibit significantly lower corrosion rates (as measured by mass loss, pit depth, and surface degradation via spectroscopic methods) compared to baseline samples with nominal oxide coverage. In contrast, samples where the oxide film is removed/disrupted will show accelerated corrosion even if the microstructure is otherwise optimized.
generation.baseline: Standard steel samples that have undergone typical processing, resulting in a natural but unmodified oxide film and microstructure.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is testable for steels operating in environments typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications under moderate to high temperatures (450–700 °C) and within controlled ionizing radiation doses. It may not hold in environments significantly outside these conditions or under long-term exposure regimes that could promote phase instabilities not accounted for in this study.
generation.uncertainty: While the protective role of Cr2O3 in corrosion resistance is well documented, the relative quantitative contributions of the passive film versus the microstructural effects (e.g., grain boundary diffusion) remain uncertain. Additionally, the interaction between radiation-induced damage and oxide film stability could introduce complexities not fully predictable under all service conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of steel samples: (a) one set with the natural passive oxide film intact and an optimized microstructure, and (b) a second set where the oxide layer is removed via a standardized chemical/mechanical treatment while retaining the optimized microstructure. Both sets will be subjected to identical simulated operational conditions (temperature, corrosive salt environment, and controlled radiation). Corrosion progress is monitored over time.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to evaluate passive film integrity
Surface and cross-sectional X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to assess oxide film composition and thickness
Microscopic evaluation (SEM/EDS) of corrosion pit formation and microstructural changes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the removal of the passive oxide layer does not result in a statistically significant increase in corrosion rate (or any deterioration in protective performance) compared to the baseline, or if samples with deliberately damaged oxide films continue to show similar corrosion resistance when compared to intact samples, then the hypothesis that the Cr2O3 passive film (in synergy with the microstructure) governs the observed corrosion resistance would be falsified.

Similarly, it was speculated that the Cr2O3 passivation film has the same effect in the corrosion resistance of HEAs. Therefore, for the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating passivation film of this study, it can be obtained from the results of XPS that the Cr2O3 in the passivation film provides good corrosion resistance for the coating, and the addition of trace amount of Nb results in forming a stable metal oxide of Nb2O5 in the passivation film of the coating, which also plays a positive role in the corrosion resistance [,].

cited_evidence.text: The use of HEAs in nuclear applications depends greatly on their microstructural stability in the extreme environments of the operating conditions. Although Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 alloy shows good mechanical properties and relatively high resistance to radiation damage, this study showed that the alloy experienced phase instability at 700 °C after 1000 hours. Cr-rich particles were found to precipitate in the alloy, even well beneath the corrosion affected region, after the high temperature exposure during the corrosion test. Just underneath the surface, few fine circular Cr-rich precipitates were observed. As the distance from the surface increased, the Cr-rich precipitates’ concentration increased and their morphology became more needle-shaped as shown in Fig. 6. Then, the precipitates’ concentration decreased significantly but persisted through the entire thickness of the sample as shown in Figs. 6 and 9. These changes in the concentration and morphology of the Cr-rich precipitates indicate that the precipitation process not only depends on both the annealing temperature and duration, but also on the Mn concentration in the alloy, which varies due to its dissolution in the salt.

This phenomenon is expected to have a dual effect on corrosion behavior, which is dependent upon the material/environment system, as reviewed in [,]. As a general rule, a nanocrystalline structure in passivating electrolytes exhibits an improvement in corrosion resistance, whereas in depassivating electrolytes it exhibits a decrease in corrosion resistance [,]. The effect of grain size on the corrosion behavior of HEAs has been little studied to date [,]. frame.system: Steels designed for chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, typically featuring microstructural phases (e.g., martensitic or austenitic structures) and pre-existing passive oxide layers.
frame.goal: To elucidate the mechanistic basis for enhanced corrosion resistance by identifying whether factors such as adaptive oxide film formation, specific microstructural configurations, or synergistic effects under irradiation/chemical exposure are responsible.
frame.limitation: The precise mechanism enabling these steels to resist corrosion under harsh chemical and radiation environments remains ambiguous.
constraints: Controlled study setup to isolate individual factors
Observations need to be compared relative to a baseline under standard conditions
Defined boundaries or operating regimes (chemical-processing and nuclear power specific conditions)
Corroborative evidence should align with prior findings
An outcome must exist that could clearly falsify the hypothesis
frame.regime: Simulated chemical processing and nuclear power conditions, involving high temperatures, corrosive chemical exposures, and possibly ionizing radiation to mimic service conditions.
prior_attempts: Previous studies have generally characterized corrosion resistance through surface composition analyses and long-term exposure tests without isolating the distinct roles of microstructure and oxide-layer dynamics.
Baseline corrosion testing under non-controlled variables failed to pinpoint the cause-effect relationship between environmental factors and corrosion resistance mechanisms.

families.best_lever: Differentiate the roles of microstructural phases and pre-existing oxide layers by independently varying environmental variables (e.g., radiation intensity, chemical exposure temperatures) and comparing corrosion rates.

families.best_lever: Deploy in situ synchrotron X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and transmission electron microscopy to monitor the growth and evolution of passive oxide films during exposure to simulated corrosive and irradiation conditions.

families.best_lever: Develop mesoscale models (e.g., kinetic Monte Carlo simulations) to simulate the kinetics of oxide film formation and microstructural evolution under tailored chemical and irradiation conditions.
